title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the scattered paragraph, the empty cell and the two needs

questions.prompt: These six parts, several of them incomplete on their own, make one paragraph. Put them back in order.

options.text: giving away more than four hundred thousand dinars to those schools in twelve years.
the oldest of whom are now at university.
Zeineb Ferchichi sold her printing workshop in 2014
and devoted the rest of her life to the schools of her governorate,
and founded, between 2016 and 2020, three reading clubs for the girls of those villages,

questions.explanation: Only one part can open: it names the woman in full, it carries the first date, and it is the only one that begins neither with and, nor with an -ing form, nor with a pronoun. Every other part says she, those or whom, so each of them needs something said before it. The part beginning and devoted the rest of her life adds a second verb to sold and ends on a comma, so something must still follow it. The -ing part, giving away more than four hundred thousand dinars to those schools, is that something: those schools points back at the schools of her governorate, and its full stop closes the first sentence. She opened seven village libraries then opens the second sentence, because only a part beginning with a capital can follow a full stop. The part beginning and founded needs those villages, which only the libraries have just supplied, and it too ends on a comma. That leaves the oldest of whom are now at university to close: whom asks for people, and the girls of the reading clubs are the only people in front of it. Try to move the founded part earlier and it loses its villages; try to close on it and a paragraph ends on a comma.

questions.prompt: A notice on the door of a charity's store room reads: "Volunteers ___ take one box each without asking." The notice is granting permission. Which of these four modals is it?
questions.explanation: "may" is the modal of permission, and a notice that lets volunteers help themselves without asking grants exactly that: Volunteers may take one box each. "must" would turn the permission into an obligation and order every volunteer to carry a box away, whether they wanted one or not. "should" gives advice, so it would recommend taking a box rather than allow it. "shall" goes with I and we, where it states a future the speaker commits to or offers something in a question, as in Shall I carry it for you?, and it does not open a door to anybody else.

questions.prompt: In the same three-column table, one row reads: (Verb) ___ · (Noun) philanthropy · (Adjective) philanthropic. What belongs in the empty cell?
questions.explanation: Some rows of a word-family table have an empty cell, and this is one of them: English builds "no verb at all" on philanthropy. You say to do philanthropic work, or to give to a good cause, and the emptiness is a fact of the language, not an oversight of the printer. "philanthropist" is a real word, but it names the person who gives, and a person belongs in a fourth column that this table does not have. "philanthropise" copies the -ise of organise and modernise, and "philanthropate" copies the -ate of donate, onto a noun that accepts neither ending. The same thing happens with charity: the adjective is charitable, and there is no ordinary verb there either.

questions.prompt: In which of these three sentences does set off carry the meaning "make somebody suddenly very angry"? (1) The climbers set off before sunrise. (2) One remark about the money set her off. (3) A dropped match set off the fire alarm.
questions.explanation: set off carries three different meanings in these three sentences, and "only (2)" is the one whose object is a person: one remark set her off, that is, made her suddenly very angry. Sentence (1) uses the commonest meaning of all, starting a journey, and there it takes no object whatever. Sentence (3) uses the second, triggering a device or a reaction, and its object is a machine, not a temper. "only (1) and (3)" groups those two together, which is a fair grouping in itself, since neither of them is about anybody's feelings — but that is precisely why neither can be the answer. The object gives the meaning away every time: a person for the anger, a device for the trigger, nothing at all for the journey.

questions.prompt: Two notes are pinned side by side in a village dispensary. (1) "Mrs Aloui ran the pharmacy for eleven years." (2) "Mr Gharbi has run the pharmacy for eleven years." Which of the two is still behind the counter?
questions.explanation: for eleven years measures a length and settles nothing on its own: it is the tense on either side of it that says whether the period reaches today. has run is a present perfect, so Mr Gharbi's eleven years come right up to now and he is still there — "Mr Gharbi only". ran is a simple past, so Mrs Aloui's eleven years are shut inside the past and she has left the counter. "Both pharmacists" trusts for on its own, which is exactly the trap the two notes were written to set. "Neither pharmacist" reads eleven years as a quantity that has been used up, but a length is not an end. "Mrs Aloui only" reverses the two tenses exactly.

questions.prompt: One idea, two shapes. The first is: "Parents have to be understanding; otherwise they may have communication problems with their children." Which sentence built on if says the same thing?

options.text: If parents won't be understanding, they may have communication problems with their children.
If parents were not understanding, they may have communication problems with their children.
If parents aren't understanding, they may have communication problems with their children.
If parents are understanding, they may have communication problems with their children.

questions.explanation: otherwise announces what follows when the first half is not respected, so the rewrite has to carry that failure into the if-clause: "If parents aren't understanding, they may have communication problems with their children." "If parents are understanding, ..." drops the negation that otherwise was carrying, and ends up promising the problems to the very parents who do it right. "If parents won't be understanding, ..." puts a future inside an if-clause, which English refuses however future the warning feels. "If parents were not understanding, ..." moves the condition into the unreal past, the one used after wish and if only, which imagines what is contrary to fact — while may in the second half keeps this sentence firmly in the real present.
